functions.name: BT::KeepRunningUntilFailureNode::tick
functions.description: Performs one tick of the KeepRunningUntilFailure decorator. It forwards the tick to its single child and returns RUNNING unless the child returns FAILURE. Specifically: if the child returns FAILURE, the decorator resets its child and returns FAILURE; if the child returns SUCCESS, it resets the child and returns RUNNING; if the child returns RUNNING, it returns RUNNING. Intended to be called by the BehaviorTree executor while the node is part of a valid tree.
requirements: This node must have exactly one initialized child before tick() is called (inferred from DecoratorNode semantics and the use of child_node_->executeTick()).
The child must be in a state where executeTick() is valid (initialized/constructed by the tree).
Callers should expect only BT::NodeStatus::FAILURE or BT::NodeStatus::RUNNING as return values; BT::NodeStatus::SUCCESS is never returned by this function (explicit from implementation).

functions.name: BT::LoopNode::tick
functions.description: Ticks the LoopNode decorator: pops the front element from the input queue port "queue" (a SharedQueue<T>), writes it to the output port "value", and executes the single child as long as items are available. If the child returns RUNNING, the same item is not popped again until the child completes. If no item is popped and the child is not running, the node returns the status specified by the "if_empty" input port (default SUCCESS). Intended to be used by BehaviorTree.CPP as a Decorator with exactly one child.
requirements: Node must be configured with a single child (DecoratorNode contract).
Input port "queue" must contain either a SharedQueue<T> stored on the blackboard (as a pointer-like entry) or a string that can be converted to SharedQueue<T> via convertFromString specializations.
Input port "if_empty" is optional; if absent, defaults to BT::NodeStatus::SUCCESS.
Output port "value" must be available to receive the popped T value each iteration when an element is popped.
The node modifies the queue (pop_front) when the child is not RUNNING; callers relying on the queue contents must account for mutation.
Type T must be registered with the factory if it is not Any, std::string, or double (as noted), otherwise port conversions/registrations may fail (exact registration mechanism outside this header).

The tree (and subscribed nodes) should remain alive while this logger is alive so that stored subscription tokens remain valid and callbacks can be received.
Construction subscribes immediately; any status changes during/after construction may trigger callback().
Timestamps passed to callback() will be BT::Duration values representing either time_since_epoch() (absolute) or time since the first observed timestamp (relative).

Initial internal state: enabled is true; timestamp type defaults to BT::TimestampType::absolute; the transition-to-IDLE visibility is initialized to true in this constructor (note: a comment above suggests 'false by default', which conflicts with the constructor’s initialization).

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::~StatusChangeLogger
functions.description: Virtual destructor for StatusChangeLogger. Allows safe deletion via a base-pointer and ensures stored subscription tokens are destroyed, which typically unsubscribes from node status changes.
requirements: Must be called (implicitly or explicitly) when the logger is no longer needed; ensure no external threads are concurrently using a derived object past its lifetime.
Derived classes should ensure any resources buffered for output are flushed (e.g., from flush()) before destruction if needed.

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::callback
functions.signature: void BT::StatusChangeLogger::callback(BT::Duration timestamp, const BT::TreeNode& node, BT::NodeStatus prev_status, BT::NodeStatus status)
functions.description: Pure virtual hook invoked on each subscribed node’s status transition. The timestamp is a BT::Duration representing either an absolute time (since epoch) or a relative time since the first observed event, depending on the current TimestampType. Implement this in derived classes to perform logging or other handling of status changes.
requirements: Must be implemented by derived classes (pure virtual).
Implementations must accept that calls can occur from subscription contexts and may be concurrent across different node updates; ensure any internal state usage is thread-safe as needed.
The node reference is const and must not be modified.
prev_status and status are BT::NodeStatus enumeration values representing the transition; implementations must handle cases including transitions to IDLE if enabled by enableTransitionToIdle().
Should not assume timestamp is monotonic across different clocks beyond what BT::Duration provides; interpret it according to the current TimestampType setting.

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::flush
functions.description: Pure virtual method intended to flush any buffered log output or finalize pending logging actions in derived classes.
requirements: Must be implemented by derived classes (pure virtual).
May be called when the user needs to force output completion; implementations should be reentrant or otherwise safely callable relative to callback().

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::setEnabled
functions.description: Enables or disables delivery of status-change events to the callback. When disabled, transitions are ignored (except internal bookkeeping).
requirements: Can be called at any time to toggle logging; value true enables callbacks, false suppresses them.

Callers should be aware that this method does not use the internal callback mutex; if called concurrently with active callbacks, rely on the benign data race semantics of reading/writing a bool or externally synchronize if stronger guarantees are required.

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::setTimestampType
functions.description: Sets the timestamp interpretation used for subsequent callback invocations. absolute passes the time since epoch; relative passes the time elapsed since the first observed timestamp after construction.
requirements: type must be either BT::TimestampType::absolute or BT::TimestampType::relative.
May be called at any time; it affects only future callbacks, not previously delivered ones.

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::enabled
functions.description: Returns whether the logger is currently enabled for delivering callback notifications.
requirements: None; callable at any time and thread-safe to read the current flag.

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::showsTransitionToIdle
functions.description: Returns whether transitions to the IDLE status are included in callbacks. A code comment claims this is false by default, but the constructor sets the flag to true in this header, so the initial value is effectively true here.
requirements: None; callable at any time.

functions.name: BT::StatusChangeLogger::enableTransitionToIdle
functions.description: Enables or disables delivery of callbacks for transitions where the new status is IDLE. When disabled, only non-IDLE transitions trigger the callback.
requirements: May be called at any time to change inclusion of IDLE transitions.
Set enable to true to include IDLE transitions; false to suppress them.

functions.name: BT::StdCoutLogger::StdCoutLogger
functions.description: Constructs a StdCoutLogger that subscribes to status-change events from the given BehaviorTree and prints node transitions to standard output. Use this to monitor a tree's execution in real time from the console. Internally leverages StatusChangeLogger to receive callbacks.
requirements: Argument tree must refer to a valid, initialized BT::Tree instance.
The referenced BT::Tree must outlive the BT::StdCoutLogger instance (tree is held by reference).
Thread-safety or reentrancy guarantees are unknown; avoid calling from multiple threads unless the underlying library documents it as safe.

functions.name: BT::StdCoutLogger::~StdCoutLogger
functions.description: Destroys the StdCoutLogger, terminating its subscription to status-change events and cleaning up associated resources. Intended to stop console logging when the logger goes out of scope or is no longer needed.
requirements: Must not be invoked while other threads are concurrently using the same BT::StdCoutLogger instance (thread-safety unspecified).
Any references or pointers to this logger must not be used after destruction.

functions.name: BT::StdCoutLogger::flush
functions.description: Forces the logger to flush any buffered console output. Use to ensure that all pending transition messages are written to stdout immediately (e.g., before program termination or when synchronizing logs). Exact buffering behavior is not documented and may be implementation-dependent.
requirements: May be called at any time during the logger's lifetime; must not be called after destruction.
No arguments required; return value indicates no error reporting via this API.

functions.signature: BT::FileLogger2::FileLogger2(const BT::Tree& tree, const std::filesystem::path& filepath)
functions.description: Constructs a file-based behavior tree logger that writes the tree (as XML) and subsequent node status transitions to a file, using a background thread to minimize latency. requirements: filepath must have the .btlog suffix; otherwise this constructor throws (as documented).
The provided filepath should be a valid path where a file can be created and written (inferred from file logging).
tree is passed by const reference and is expected to refer to the tree being logged for the lifetime of the logger (inferred from typical logger usage).
Exceptions: callers should be prepared to handle exceptions thrown by the constructor when validation (e.g., suffix) fails or when file opening fails (inferred).

functions.name: BT::FileLogger2::~FileLogger2
functions.description: Destroys the logger, stopping background logging and finalizing any pending writes. Given data is written on a separate thread, destruction is expected to stop the writer thread and close the output file cleanly.
requirements: After destruction, the logger must no longer be used.
Callers should ensure no concurrent use is in progress at the time of destruction (inferred from background thread usage).

functions.name: BT::FileLogger2::callback
functions.signature: void BT::FileLogger2::callback(BT::Duration timestamp, const BT::TreeNode& node, BT::NodeStatus prev_status, BT::NodeStatus status)
functions.description: Receives a node status change event and queues/writes it to the log. The event contains a timestamp, the affected node, its previous status, and its new status. This overrides StatusChangeLogger::callback and is typically invoked by the BehaviorTree.CPP framework, not by user code.
requirements: timestamp must represent the event time in the same unit/epoch convention used by the logger (microseconds since epoch is used in file format; exact Duration definition is per library).
node must refer to a valid TreeNode belonging to the associated tree (inferred from logger purpose).
prev_status and status must be valid BT::NodeStatus values.
Reentrancy/concurrency: external callers should avoid calling this directly while the logger is operating unless following the library’s threading model (inferred).

functions.name: BT::FileLogger2::flush
functions.description: Forces any buffered log data to be written to the output file. Overrides StatusChangeLogger::flush. Useful to ensure on-disk consistency at specific points while the logger is alive.
requirements: May be called at any time during the lifetime of the logger to ensure pending data is written.
Callers should expect that flush may block until the background writer has persisted outstanding data (inferred).

functions.name: BT::MinitraceLogger::MinitraceLogger
functions.description: Constructs a MinitraceLogger that records status changes from the given behavior tree and writes them to a JSON trace file. Use this to attach a minitrace-compatible logger to an existing BT::Tree; events are typically produced by the BehaviorTree.CPP runtime.
requirements: tree must reference a valid BT::Tree that remains alive and unchanged in memory for at least as long as the logger instance exists (inferred from passing by const reference and typical logger patterns).
filename_json must be a non-null pointer to a null-terminated C string representing the output JSON file path.
The process must have permission to create or write to filename_json; if the file cannot be opened or written, logging may fail (behavior not specified in header).
Thread-safety and ownership of the BT::Tree are unspecified; do not mutate or destroy the tree from another thread while the logger is operating unless the underlying library guarantees safety.

functions.name: BT::MinitraceLogger::~MinitraceLogger
functions.description: Destructor for MinitraceLogger. Cleans up any resources associated with the logger (e.g., closing files, flushing buffers). Typically invoked automatically when the logger goes out of scope.
requirements: Do not use the MinitraceLogger instance after the destructor has run.
If multithreaded logging is in use, ensure no concurrent calls into this instance during destruction (thread-safety unspecified).

functions.name: BT::MinitraceLogger::callback
functions.signature: virtual void BT::MinitraceLogger::callback(Duration timestamp, const TreeNode& node, NodeStatus prev_status, NodeStatus status)
functions.description: Override invoked on node status transitions to record an event into the minitrace log. Normally called by the BehaviorTree.CPP framework rather than user code.
requirements: timestamp must be a valid Duration value; time origin and monotonicity are unspecified in this header.
node must be a valid reference to a TreeNode that belongs to the associated BT::Tree and is alive for the duration of the call.
prev_status and status must be valid NodeStatus enumeration values; their specific allowed combinations are not specified here.
Intended to be called by the framework; external callers should avoid invoking it directly unless emulating framework behavior.

functions.name: BT::MinitraceLogger::flush
functions.description: Flushes any buffered trace data to the underlying output (e.g., the JSON file). Call this to ensure events are persisted.
requirements: The MinitraceLogger instance must be valid (not destroyed) when calling flush.
No guarantees on thread-safety are provided; avoid concurrent modification or calls from multiple threads unless documented elsewhere.
Frequency and cost of flush are unspecified; excessive flushing may impact performance.

functions.name: BT::TreeObserver::TreeObserver
functions.description: Constructs a TreeObserver that attaches to the given BehaviorTree to collect per-node execution statistics (last result/status, transition counts, timestamps). Typically used for testing or monitoring by observing status change callbacks from the tree.

The referenced tree should outlive the TreeObserver instance (inferred from typical logger/observer lifetime semantics)

Thread-safety and concurrent ticking/registration behavior are unspecified; external synchronization may be required (unknown)

functions.name: BT::TreeObserver::~TreeObserver
functions.description: Destroys the TreeObserver and stops collecting statistics. If it registered callbacks with the tree, those registrations are released during destruction.
requirements: The TreeObserver should be destroyed before the observed BT::Tree if the observer holds registrations into the tree (inferred; exact lifetime requirements are not documented)
Any references previously obtained from getStatistics(), statistics(), pathToUID(), or uidToPath() must not be used after destruction

functions.name: BT::TreeObserver::flush
functions.description: No-op flush override. Provided to satisfy the StatusChangeLogger interface; calling it has no effect.
requirements: None

functions.name: BT::TreeObserver::resetStatistics
functions.description: Clears or reinitializes the collected per-node statistics. Use to start a fresh measurement window without rebuilding the observer.
requirements: Do not use previously obtained references to NodeStatistics (from getStatistics) or to the statistics() container across a call to resetStatistics; they may become invalid if the underlying storage is cleared/rebuilt (inferred)

functions.signature: const BT::TreeObserver::NodeStatistics& BT::TreeObserver::getStatistics(const std::string& path) const
functions.description: Returns a const reference to the collected statistics for the node identified by its tree path string.

Caller must not attempt to modify the returned statistics (const)

Caller must not attempt to modify the returned container (const)

functions.name: BT::TreeObserver::pathToUID

functions.name: BT::TreeObserver::uidToPath
functions.description: Returns a const reference to the mapping from node UIDs to node path strings known to the observer.
requirements: The returned reference is only valid while the TreeObserver is alive; do not use it after destruction (inferred)

functions.name: BT::SqliteLogger::SqliteLogger
functions.signature: BT::SqliteLogger::SqliteLogger(const BT::Tree& tree, const std::filesystem::path& file, bool append = false)
functions.description: Constructs a SQLite-backed logger that records the provided behavior tree definition and all node status transitions into a single SQLite database file. To be readable by Groot2, the output filename must use the “.db3” suffix; the constructor will throw otherwise. If append is true, the logger appends a new recording session to the same database file, assigning a unique session_id.
requirements: file must use the .db3 suffix; otherwise this constructor will throw (as documented in the header comments).
tree should be a valid BT::Tree to be logged; exact lifetime requirements relative to the logger are unknown (not stated).
append determines whether a new session is appended to an existing DB (true) or a fresh one is created (false).
Behavior on unwritable paths or database open errors is unknown (not specified).

functions.name: BT::SqliteLogger::~SqliteLogger
functions.description: Destructor for the SqliteLogger. Cleans up logger resources and stops any internal background work (e.g., writer thread) associated with logging to the SQLite database. Typical users don’t need to call anything special besides destroying the object when finished logging.
requirements: No explicit caller requirements are documented.
Do not use the object after destruction.

functions.name: BT::SqliteLogger::setAdditionalCallback
functions.signature: void BT::SqliteLogger::setAdditionalCallback(std::function<std::string(BT::Duration, const BT::TreeNode&, BT::NodeStatus, BT::NodeStatus)> func)
functions.description: Installs an extra callback used to generate an additional string payload stored in the Transitions table’s extra_data column for each recorded transition. The function is invoked with the same arguments as callback() and should return the string to store.
requirements: func must be callable with (BT::Duration timestamp, const BT::TreeNode& node, BT::NodeStatus prev_status, BT::NodeStatus status) and return std::string.
The callback may be invoked for each status transition; ensure it can be called frequently. Threading context is not specified; thread-safety requirements are unknown.
If no callback is set, no extra_data will be added (implied).

functions.name: BT::SqliteLogger::callback
functions.signature: void BT::SqliteLogger::callback(BT::Duration timestamp, const BT::TreeNode& node, BT::NodeStatus prev_status, BT::NodeStatus status)
functions.description: Status-change notification handler overriding StatusChangeLogger::callback. Records the transition for the specified node at the given time, optionally augmenting it with extra_data from the installed ExtraCallback. Normally invoked by the BehaviorTree logging framework rather than called directly by user code.
requirements: timestamp should represent the time of the transition; exact units for BT::Duration are determined by the library and are not specified here.
node should refer to a node that belongs to the same tree being logged (inferred from purpose).
prev_status and status should be valid BT::NodeStatus values.
Typical callers should not call this directly; it is intended to be used by the framework (inferred from override and logger pattern).

functions.name: BT::SqliteLogger::execSqlStatement
functions.description: Executes the provided SQL statement against the logger’s underlying SQLite database connection. Useful for issuing custom commands or queries beyond the automatic logging operations.
requirements: statement should be a valid SQL statement for SQLite; behavior on invalid SQL is not specified.
Must be called on a successfully constructed SqliteLogger with an open database (implied).
Side effects on the predefined schema are the caller’s responsibility; no safeguards are documented.

functions.name: BT::SqliteLogger::flush
functions.description: Forces pending log data to be written to the SQLite database. Use this to ensure that queued transitions are persisted at a specific point in time.
requirements: No explicit requirements documented.
Call when you need to force persistence of pending transitions; exact blocking semantics are unspecified.

functions.description: Return a short string literal name for the given RequestType (e.g., FULLTREE -> "full_tree"). Intended for logging/serialization of request kinds. Unknown/unsupported enum values map to "undefined".
requirements: Argument must be a valid BT::Monitor::RequestType value; unsupported values will return "undefined".
The returned pointer refers to a static string literal; do not free or modify it.

functions.name: BT::Monitor::RequestHeader::size
functions.description: Return the serialized byte size of a RequestHeader when transmitted (protocol + type + unique_id). Used to size buffers for (de)serialization.
requirements: None; this function is pure and side-effect free.
The returned value is currently 6 (2x uint8_t + 1x uint32_t) based on the header’s definition.

functions.name: BT::Monitor::Serialize
functions.signature: template <typename T> unsigned BT::Monitor::Serialize(char* buffer, unsigned offset, T value)
functions.description: Serialize a trivially copyable value T into a raw byte buffer at the given offset using memcpy. Returns the number of bytes written (sizeof(T)). Suitable for composing contiguous message buffers.
requirements: T must be trivially copyable (memcpy-safe).
buffer must be a valid, writable memory region; the range [buffer + offset, buffer + offset + sizeof(T)) must be accessible.
No bounds checking is performed; caller must ensure sufficient capacity before calling.
Serialization uses the platform’s native endianness and object representation; cross-platform interchange may require explicit byte order handling.

functions.name: BT::Monitor::Deserialize
functions.signature: template <typename T> unsigned BT::Monitor::Deserialize(const char* buffer, unsigned offset, T& value)
functions.description: Deserialize a trivially copyable value T from a raw byte buffer at the given offset using memcpy. Stores the result into value and returns the number of bytes read (sizeof(T)).
requirements: T must be trivially copyable (memcpy-safe).
buffer must be a valid, readable memory region; the range [buffer + offset, buffer + offset + sizeof(T)) must be accessible.
No bounds checking is performed; caller must ensure sufficient data is available before calling.
Deserialization assumes the platform’s native endianness and object representation matching the producer.

functions.name: BT::Monitor::SerializeHeader
functions.description: Serialize a RequestHeader into a compact 6-byte string (protocol, type, unique_id) using native layout via memcpy. Intended as the first frame of a multipart message.
requirements: None on input aside from a valid RequestHeader object.
Output string size is exactly 6 bytes; consumers must expect this size.
Serialization uses native endianness and layout; only interoperable with matching DeserializeRequestHeader.

functions.name: BT::Monitor::DeserializeRequestHeader
functions.description: Parse a 6-byte buffer into a RequestHeader (protocol, type, unique_id) using memcpy. Converts the type byte to a RequestType enum.
requirements: buffer.size() must be at least 6 bytes; no explicit size check is performed.
Buffer contents must be produced by the corresponding SerializeHeader(RequestHeader) and share the same endianness.
If the type byte does not correspond to a known RequestType, the result will contain RequestType::UNDEFINED.

functions.name: BT::Monitor::DeserializeReplyHeader
functions.description: Parse a 22-byte buffer into a ReplyHeader by first deserializing the embedded RequestHeader (first 6 bytes) and then the 16-byte tree UUID.
requirements: buffer.size() must be at least 22 bytes; no explicit size check is performed.
Buffer contents must be produced by SerializeHeader(ReplyHeader) and share the same endianness.
The first 6 bytes must form a valid serialized RequestHeader; the next 16 bytes are taken verbatim as the tree UUID.

functions.name: BT::Groot2Publisher::Groot2Publisher
functions.description: Constructs a Groot2Publisher that bridges a BT.CPP Tree execution to the Groot2 UI via a TCP server on the given port. Ensure no external threads are concurrently invoking publisher methods during destruction (object must not be used after it begins destruction).

May be called after construction and before/while a connection is active; thread-safety is not specified in this header.

functions.name: BT::Groot2Publisher::maxHeartbeatDelay
functions.description: Returns the currently configured maximum allowed heartbeat gap before the publisher treats the Groot2 connection as lost. Defaults to 5000 ms if not changed.
requirements: Object must be valid; callable on a const instance.
Return value is the configured delay; no additional side effects.

import random
import string
from typing import List

# Target: Generate interesting arbitrary text buffers that will be fed to
# FUZZ_PARAM_STR() and FUZZ_PARAM_FILENAME() in many stubs. The data should
# be valid strings exercising different code paths: XML-like, JSON-like,
# key=value lists, semicolon-separated tokens, blackboard pointers {key},
# numeric tokens, wildcard patterns, filenames with extensions used by
# the stubs (.btlog), and script-like snippets.
#
# We keep total size <= 4096 bytes.

MAX_SIZE = 4096

def _rand_choice(r: random.Random, seq):
    return seq[r.randrange(len(seq))]

def _weighted_choice(r: random.Random, items):
    # items: list of (weight, value)
    total = sum(w for w, _ in items)
    x = r.uniform(0, total)
    acc = 0.0
    for w, v in items:
        acc += w
        if x <= acc:
            return v
    return items[-1][1]

SAFE_CHARS = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + " _-:/.,{}[]()<>=+*?;\n\t"  # printable set used across stubs

WILDCARDS = [
    "*", "?", "**/*", "*.xml", "node_*", "**/path/*",
]

def make_xml(r: random.Random) -> str:
    # Minimal XML-like snippets used by XMLParser/VerifyXML
    attrs = [
        'ID="{id}"', 'msec="{msec}"', 'delay_msec="{msec}"',
        'success_count="{n}"', 'failure_count="{n}"',
    ]
    idv = ''.join(r.choice(string.ascii_letters + string.digits) for _ in range(r.randint(3,10)))
    msec = r.randint(0, 1500)
    n = r.randint(-1, 5)
    attr = _rand_choice(r, attrs).format(id=idv, msec=msec, n=n)
    # Sometimes include builtin nodes the factory knows (AlwaysSuccess/AlwaysFailure)
    node_tag = _rand_choice(r, ["AlwaysSuccess", "AlwaysFailure", "Sleep", "Timeout", "SetBlackboard", "SubTree"])
    ports = ""
    if node_tag == "Sleep":
        ports = f" msec=\"{msec}\""
    if node_tag == "Timeout":
        ports = f" msec=\"{msec}\""
    if node_tag == "SetBlackboard":
        # map value and output_key; value can reference a blackboard pointer
        val = _rand_choice(r, ["42", "hello", "{src}"])
        ports = f" value=\"{val}\" output_key=\"dst\""
    inner = f"<{node_tag}{ports}/>"
    tree_name = _rand_choice(r, ["MainTree", "T", "root"]) + ("_" + idv if r.random()<0.3 else "")
    return f"<root {attr}><BehaviorTree ID=\"{tree_name}\">{inner}</BehaviorTree></root>"

def make_json(r: random.Random) -> str:
    # Simple JSON array or object with ints/strings
    if r.random() < 0.5:
        arr = [str(r.randint(-1000, 1000)) for _ in range(r.randint(0, 6))]
        return "[" + ", ".join(arr) + "]"
    else:
        key = ''.join(r.choice(string.ascii_lowercase) for _ in range(r.randint(3,8)))
        val = ''.join(r.choice(string.ascii_letters) for _ in range(r.randint(3,8)))
        return f"{{\"{key}\": \"{val}\"}}"

def make_semicolon_list(r: random.Random) -> str:
    # Used by convertFromString SharedQueue specializations
    kind = r.randrange(4)
    n = r.randint(0, 8)
    toks: List[str] = []
    for _ in range(n):
        if kind == 0:
            toks.append(str(r.randint(-1000, 1000)))
        elif kind == 1:
            toks.append(_rand_choice(r, ["true", "false", "1", "0"]))
        elif kind == 2:
            toks.append(f"{r.randint(-1000,1000)}.{r.randint(0,999):03d}")
        else:
            s = ''.join(r.choice(string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "_:") for _ in range(r.randint(0, 12)))
            toks.append(s)
    return ";".join(toks)

def make_blackboard_pointer(r: random.Random) -> str:
    key = ''.join(r.choice(string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "_:/") for _ in range(r.randint(1, 12)))
    return "{" + key + "}"

def make_script(r: random.Random) -> str:
    # Small scripting snippets used by ScriptNode/PreconditionNode
    choices = [
        "true", "false", "1", "0",
        "bb.set('x',1)",
        "bb.set('y',0)",
        "(2+2)==4",
        "bb.get('z') == 3",
    ]
    base = _rand_choice(r, choices)
    if r.random() < 0.3:
        # combine two with semicolon
        base = base + "; " + _rand_choice(r, choices)
    return base

import json
import random
import struct
from typing import List

# We need to generate an initial buffer that the fuzzing harness will split
# into FUZZ_PARAM primitives. The stub uses:
# - FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)
# - FUZZ_PARAM(int)
# - FUZZ_PARAM(double)
# - FUZZ_PARAM_STR()
# The harness is expected to read them in this order (first selection mode, then
# one of the typed values or string). We will encode a simple self-describing
# stream so that many common fuzzers (that treat the whole buffer as raw bytes)
# still provide deterministic data to those extractors.
#
# Since we cannot control the harness’ exact decoding, our best strategy is to
# craft buffers that contain plausible representations of these primitives in
# sequence, multiple times, so whichever way the harness slices bytes, it
# frequently lands on sensible values. We will:
# - Start with a 4-byte mode selector (0,1,2) to bias the first FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int).
# - Then include triplets: [int32, float64, length-prefixed UTF-8 string],
#   repeated a few times, to supply data for subsequent FUZZ_PARAM calls.
# - Strings will be short (<=128) ASCII/UTF-8 to keep allocations small and
#   valid for JSON quoting.
# - We randomize values but keep them within reasonable ranges to avoid
#   corner cases like NaNs unless intentionally chosen.
#
# The buffer size will be kept <= 4096 bytes.

_DEF_STRS = [
    "hello",
    "42",
    "-13",
    "3.14159",
    "true",
    "false",
    "null",
    "{key}",
    "line\nfeed",
    "quote:\"backslash:\\",
]


def _rand_string(rng: random.Random, max_len: int = 64) -> str:
    # Mix of alphanum, spaces, punctuation, and some escapables
    alphabet = (
        "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789 "
        "_-:/.,{}[]()!@#$%^&*?=+\t\n\r\"\\"
    )
    # Choose either a canned interesting string or a random one
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        s = rng.choice(_DEF_STRS)
    else:
        n = rng.randint(0, max_len)
        s = "".join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(n))
    # Ensure it is valid UTF-8 once encoded
    return s


def _pack_triplet(i: int, d: float, s: str) -> bytes:
    # int32, float64, uint16 length, bytes
    b = struct.pack("<i", i)
    b += struct.pack("<d", d)
    sb = s.encode("utf-8", errors="ignore")
    if len(sb) > 512:
        sb = sb[:512]
    b += struct.pack("<H", len(sb))
    b += sb
    return b


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Decide first mode to help the stub select type: 0=int,1=double,2=string
    mode = rng.randrange(0, 3)
    out = bytearray()
    out += struct.pack("<I", mode)

    # Create several triplets to satisfy subsequent FUZZ_PARAMs regardless of order
    triplets: List[bytes] = []

    # Seed with a few canonical values to exercise boundaries
    canon_ints = [0, 1, -1, 1000, -1000, 2**31 - 1, -2**31]
    canon_doubles = [0.0, 1.0, -1.0, 1e-9, -1e-9, 1e9, -1e9, 3.141592653589793]
    canon_strs = [
        "",
        "0",
        "-12",
        "3.14",
        "1e-9",
        "simple",
        "with spaces",
        "need\\escape\"",
        "emoji 😀",
    ]

    for i in canon_ints[:3]:
        d = rng.choice(canon_doubles)
        s = rng.choice(canon_strs)
        triplets.append(_pack_triplet(i, d, s))

    # Add randomized triplets
    count = rng.randint(5, 12)
    for _ in range(count):
        # Integers in a reasonable range; mix extremes sometimes
        if rng.random() < 0.2:
            i = rng.choice(canon_ints)
        else:
            i = rng.randint(-10_000, 10_000)
        # Doubles: sometimes normal, sometimes large/small
        if rng.random() < 0.2:
            d = rng.choice(canon_doubles)
        else:
            mant = rng.uniform(-1e6, 1e6)
            d = mant / (10 ** rng.randint(0, 6))
        s = _rand_string(rng, max_len=128)
        triplets.append(_pack_triplet(i, d, s))

    # Concatenate triplets
    for t in triplets:
        out += t
        if len(out) > 3500:
            break

    # Append an optional JSON preview region to help any text-based readers.
    # It contains a compact JSON value matching the selected mode.
    try:
        if mode == 0:
            jv = rng.randint(-1000, 1000)
        elif mode == 1:
            jv = rng.choice([0.0, 1.23, -4.5, 3.14159, rng.uniform(-1e6, 1e6)])
        else:
            # Keep JSON string short; escaping will be done by stub.
            jv = _rand_string(rng, max_len=32)
        jtxt = json.dumps(jv, ensure_ascii=False)
        jb = jtxt.encode("utf-8")
        if len(jb) > 256:
            jb = jb[:256]
        # Prefix with a recognizable tag and length
        tag = b"JTAG"
        out += tag + struct.pack("<H", len(jb)) + jb
    except Exception:
        pass

    # Ensure maximum size
    if len(out) > 4096:
        out = out[:4096]

    return bytes(out)

# This generator targets inputs for BT::convertFromJSON fuzzer stub.
# The stub may choose one of: integer JSON, double JSON, or string JSON (quoted).
# We provide a bytes buffer that the harness will slice into FUZZ_PARAM and FUZZ_PARAM_STR.
# Strategy: encode a small header selecting the mode and provide coherent payloads:
# - mode 0: integer number in ASCII (possibly with sign, different magnitudes)
# - mode 1: floating-point in ASCII (normal, scientific, special-like but JSON-friendly numbers)
# - mode 2: JSON string with varied escaping, unicode, control chars escaped, etc.
# Keep total size <= 4096 bytes.

MAX_BYTES = 4096

def _rand_ascii_str(rng: random.Random, min_len: int, max_len: int) -> str:
    length = rng.randint(min_len, max_len)
    # Include a wide range of characters likely to be interesting when escaped in JSON
    pool = (
        string.ascii_letters + string.digits + string.punctuation + " "
    )
    s = ''.join(rng.choice(pool) for _ in range(length))
    return s

def _rand_unicode_str(rng: random.Random, min_len: int, max_len: int) -> str:
    length = rng.randint(min_len, max_len)
    # Mix ASCII with some selected unicode ranges
    def rand_char():
        choice = rng.random()
        if choice < 0.7:
            return rng.choice(string.ascii_letters + string.digits + string.punctuation + " ")
        elif choice < 0.85:
            # Latin-1 supplement
            return chr(rng.randint(0x00A0, 0x00FF))
        elif choice < 0.95:
            # Greek/Cyrillic
            return chr(rng.randint(0x0370, 0x052F))
        else:
            # Emoji range subset
            return chr(rng.randint(0x1F600, 0x1F64F))
    return ''.join(rand_char() for _ in range(length))

def _json_string_payload(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Construct a JSON string with various escapes and substrings resembling paths, quotes, etc.
    parts = []
    # Start with some plain text
    parts.append(_rand_unicode_str(rng, 0, 16))
    # Insert escaped sequences
    escapes = ['"', '\\', '\b', '\f', '\n', '\r', '\t']
    literal_chunks = [
        'path: C:\\\\temp\\\\file.txt',
        'quote: \"Hello\"',
        'json: {\\"k\\":123}',
        'slashes: \\\\\\\\\\\n',
    ]
    # control chars to be escaped via json.dumps automatically if present
    controls = ''.join(chr(c) for c in [0,7,8,9,10,13,27])
    parts.append(controls)
    for _ in range(rng.randint(1,3)):
        parts.append(rng.choice(literal_chunks))
    parts.append(_rand_unicode_str(rng, 0, 32))
    s = ''.join(parts)

    # Randomly sprinkle direct characters that require escaping
    for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 5)):
        s += rng.choice(['"', '\\'])
    # Ensure not too long
    if len(s) > 256:
        s = s[:256]

    # Use json.dumps to ensure valid JSON string encoding
    json_text = json.dumps(s, ensure_ascii=False)
    return json_text.encode('utf-8')

def _json_int_payload(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Choose varied integer formats (within JSON number spec – no leading zeros unless zero)
    choices = []
    # small ints
    choices.extend([str(rng.randint(-1000, 1000)) for _ in range(5)])
    # large magnitudes
    big_vals = [
        rng.randint(0, 2**31-1),
        rng.randint(0, 2**63-1),
    ]
    big_vals += [-v for v in big_vals]
    choices.extend(str(v) for v in big_vals)
    # zero and negative zero variants ("-0" is valid JSON number though rare)
    choices.extend(["0", "-0"][0:1 + int(rng.random() < 0.5)])
    return rng.choice(choices).encode('ascii')

def _json_float_payload(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Build JSON-compatible floating representations (no NaN/inf as JSON disallows them)
    vals = []
    # simple decimals
    for _ in range(3):
        v = rng.uniform(-1e6, 1e6)
        vals.append(f"{v:.6f}")
    # scientific notation
    for exp in [-12,-6,-3,0,3,6,12]:
        base = rng.uniform(-9.9, 9.9)
        vals.append(f"{base:.6e}")
    # edge-ish small/large
    vals.extend(["0.0", "-0.0", "1.0", "-1.0", "3.1415926535", "2.718281828", "1e308", "-1e308", "1e-308", "-1e-308"])
    # choose and normalize to avoid leading plus or trailing decimal dot
    s = rng.choice(vals)
    # Strip leading plus if any
    if s.startswith('+'):
        s = s[1:]
    # Ensure it parses: keep as is
    return s.encode('ascii')

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    mode = rng.randrange(3)
    if mode == 0:
        payload = _json_int_payload(rng)
    elif mode == 1:
        payload = _json_float_payload(rng)
    else:
        payload = _json_string_payload(rng)

    # The fuzzer harness uses FUZZ_PARAM_STR and others; providing just the JSON text as bytes
    # is sufficient since the stub constructs its own JSON string from FUZZ_PARAM_STR or numbers.
    # We prepend a tiny header hint that some harnesses may read; otherwise it's part of the stream.
    # Format: b"MODE:\n" then payload. This remains valid since the stub only uses FUZZ buffers independently.
    header = f"MODE={mode}\n".encode('ascii')
    out = header + payload
    if len(out) > MAX_BYTES:
        out = out[:MAX_BYTES]
    return out

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:

    sections = []

    sections.append('\n'.join(_bool_variants()))

    # 4) Semicolon lists for SharedQueue<int/bool/double/string>

    int_list = _assemble_semicolon_list(rng, [rng.randint(-1000,1000) for _ in range(10)])
    sections.append(int_list)

    bool_list = _assemble_semicolon_list(rng, _bool_variants()*2)
    sections.append(bool_list)
    # doubles
    dbl_list = _assemble_semicolon_list(rng, _numeric_variants(rng))
    sections.append(dbl_list)
    # strings (short tokens without semicolons)
    str_tokens = [
        _rand_name(rng, maxlen=8),
        "alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta",
        ''.join(rng.choice(ALNUM) for _ in range(rng.randint(1,8)))
    ]

    more_nums = [str(rng.randint(-10**9,10**9)) for _ in range(6)] + [

    sections.append('\n'.join(bads))

    # 8) Small JSON-like snippets (some consumers may ignore, but harmless)
    sections.append('{"msec":100}')

    # Assemble final buffer; cap to 4 KiB
    buf = ('\n\n'.join(sections)).encode('utf-8')
    if len(buf) > 4096:
        buf = buf[:4096]
    return buf

# Target format inferred from fuzzer stub:
# - The stub builds a semicolon-separated list of tokens of a single type among:
#   ints, bools, doubles, or strings. It expects parsing into a queue whose size
#   equals the token count. On parse error, run is discarded. Therefore we must
#   generate well-formed strings for all four cases.
# - FUZZ_PARAM_STR picks from the provided buffer. We will emit a single buffer
#   that contains one assembled line suitable for all cases; the harness will
#   slice as needed. To maximize valid runs, we primarily emit well-formed
#   semicolon-separated tokens without stray semicolons within string tokens.
# - Limit size to <= 4096 bytes.

BOOL_WORDS = ["true", "false", "1", "0"]


def _rand_int(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    # Keep within [-1000, 1000] per stub's range
    return rng.randint(-1000, 1000)


def _rand_double(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # Construct with limited precision and no inf/nan
    whole = rng.randint(-1000, 1000)
    frac = rng.randint(0, 999)
    return f"{whole}.{frac:03d}"


def _rand_bool_token(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    return rng.choice(BOOL_WORDS)


def _rand_str_token(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # Generate up to 16 chars, avoid semicolons to keep tokenization stable.
    length = rng.randint(0, 16)
    alphabet = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + " _-:.,/\\[]{}()@#%+="
    s = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(length))
    return s


def _assemble_tokens(rng: random.Random, which: int, count: int) -> str:
    tokens: List[str] = []
    for _ in range(count):
        if which == 0:  # ints
            tokens.append(str(_rand_int(rng)))
        elif which == 1:  # bools
            tokens.append(_rand_bool_token(rng))
        elif which == 2:  # doubles
            tokens.append(_rand_double(rng))
        else:  # strings
            tokens.append(_rand_str_token(rng))
    return ';'.join(tokens)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Choose which category to emit: 0=int,1=bool,2=double,3=string
    which = rng.randrange(4)
    # Up to 8 tokens to match stub; allow zero tokens too
    count = rng.randrange(0, 9)

    assembled = _assemble_tokens(rng, which, count)

    # As a bonus, sometimes emit a second variant line in the same buffer to
    # provide extra data for FUZZ_PARAM_STR consumers.
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        which2 = rng.randrange(4)
        count2 = rng.randrange(0, 9)
        assembled2 = _assemble_tokens(rng, which2, count2)
        payload = (assembled + "\n" + assembled2)[:4096]
    else:
        payload = assembled[:4096]

    return payload.encode('utf-8')

# provide inputs that are valid doubles when it chooses doubles,
# yet still syntactically harmless for other branches (they will
# be treated as one token string if chosen there).

SAFE_LEN_LIMIT = 4096

_DOUBLE_PATTERNS = [
    # plain integers (valid as doubles)
    lambda r: str(r.randint(-1000, 1000)),
    # simple fixed with decimals
    lambda r: f"{r.randint(-1000,1000)}.{r.randint(0,999):03d}",
    # leading/trailing decimal points
    lambda r: f".{r.randint(0,999999)}",
    lambda r: f"{r.randint(-1000,1000)}.",
    # scientific notation (lowercase)
    lambda r: f"{r.choice(['','-','+'])}{r.randint(0,9999)}e{r.choice(['-','+'])}{r.randint(0,308)}",
    # scientific notation (uppercase E)
    lambda r: f"{r.choice(['','-','+'])}{r.randint(0,9999)}E{r.choice(['-','+'])}{r.randint(0,308)}",
    # small/large magnitudes within double range
    lambda r: f"{r.choice(['','-'])}{r.uniform(1e-6, 1e-3):.9g}",
    lambda r: f"{r.choice(['','-'])}{r.uniform(1e3, 1e9):.9g}",
    # zeros with signs
    lambda r: r.choice(["0", "-0", "+0", "0.0", "-0.0", "+0.0"]),

    f = r.choice(_DOUBLE_PATTERNS)

def _mix_tokens(r: random.Random, n: int) -> List[str]:
    toks = []

def _assemble(tokens: List[str]) -> str:
    # Ensure no embedded semicolons within tokens; our generators don't add any.
    s = ";".join(tokens)

        # Trim by reducing token count conservatively
        # Keep at least 1 token
        cut = max(1, len(tokens) // 2)
        s = ";".join(tokens[:cut])

            s = "0.0"

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:

    # though empty count in stub means no tokens. We favor non-empty valid inputs.
    count_weights = [1] + [5]*8  # bias towards 1..8
    count_choices = list(range(0, 9))
    count = r.choices(count_choices, weights=count_weights, k=1)[0]

    tokens = _mix_tokens(r, count)

    # Occasionally craft edge-case sequences: repeating same token or alternating signs
    if count >= 2 and r.random() < 0.3:
        choice = r.randint(0, 2)
        if choice == 0:
            t = r.choice(tokens) if tokens else "0"
            tokens = [t] * count
        elif choice == 1:
            base = _gen_double_token(r)
            alt = base
            # ensure alternate sign when possible
            if not base.startswith("-"):
                alt = "-" + base
            tokens = [base if (i % 2 == 0) else alt for i in range(count)]
        else:
            # monotonically increasing magnitudes
            start = r.uniform(-10.0, 10.0)
            step = r.uniform(0.1, 5.0)
            tokens = [f"{start + i*step:.6f}" for i in range(count)]

    assembled = _assemble(tokens)
    return assembled.encode("utf-8")
